results.title: Samsung Galaxy S23 Plus with defective display.webm
results.desc: ( PHOTOSENSITIVE EPILEPSY WARNING: If you are one of the few people who experience seizures after watching flashing lights, I strongly urge you to skip, or at least play very slowly , parts 0:24 to 0:39, 0:53 to 0:55, and 0:59 to 1:04) A video of my Samsung Galaxy S23+, 256 GB, model SM-S916U, which I received last December after doing something stupid to what I think was an S21+, my previous phone. The S21+ was fairly long-lived, although it became cranky late in life when it was time to get charged, but I foolishly cut its life short when I tried to charge it while the port was still wet. That day taught me that an aged waterproofing mechanism can fail. Anyway, this result is the accumulation of LCD defects on the right side of the screen, which, if memory serves, manifested themselves by the middle of this year. First, a subtle whitish light leakage of some sort would appear along the right edge of the screen that over the months would creep ever so gradually. Then, several round clusters of dead pixels would form, which also over the months would expand slowly. Next, bright horizontal mint green lines began emanating from the middle of the dark clusters. Only one is seen in the video, but I have seen at least two simultaneous such lines before. In this video, taken on the same night that my phone's display finally began breaking, the display turned greenish and most of the bottom half of the screen experienced serious flickering issues that, interestingly, only occurred when the screen brightness was set low. Coincidentally, it is the same fate and the same shade of green that my first Android phone, which I remember having as a brand new phone as far back as November 2018 and so was presumably an S9+, suffered that led me to get the S21+. As of this upload, my dad will file an insurance claim to replace my phone. The only thing I regret when making this video is not replacing the background to a Wikipedia image. Nonetheless, the default background should pose no problems on Commons since the video subject is the phone's screen suffering defects.
